units.translation: Hence also in Aeschylus (fr. 370 N.2) they deem it right to write ‘μελανστέρφων γένος’, not, as some do, ‘μελανστέρνων’; for they have not only their chests black, but also their whole body. Hence also the jar is called στέρφος.
1366. ἀμφιλαφής: meaning variegated or large or covered with hair on both sides.
1381-82. Μουσεάων ὅδε μόχθος: inasmuch as it is invented, he says; this is the tale of the Muses, and I am the servant of the Muses. For he is inspired by them, so as to narrate.

1396-99a. ᾧ ἔνι Λάδων: Peisander (16 fr. 8 J.) supposed that the dragon was born from Earth, but Hesiod 〈...〉 says that he was from Typhon. But Agroitas in the third book of his Libyan History (fr. 3 M. IV 295) says that they were not apples, but most beautiful sheep, which were called golden; and that these had a wild shepherd, who because of his savagery was called a dragon.

b. Pherecydes in the second book (3 fr. 16a J.) says that when Hera was married, Earth brought forth apple trees bearing golden fruit, and that the nymphs, daughters of Zeus and Themis, dwelling in a cave by the Eridanus, advised Heracles in his perplexity to learn from Nereus where the golden apples were; and seizing him by force, first as he changed into water and fire, then when he returned to his former shape and revealed it, he released him. And he thus goes to the golden apples. 〈...〉 Having arrived at Tartessus he journeys to Libya, where he kills Antaeus, son of Poseidon,
